# TUI — Rule index

TUI rules are split across 5 topic files:

| File | Rules | Content |
|---------|--------|---------|
| [`tui-layout.md`](tui-layout.md) | 101, 107, 108, 111, 112, 123, 124, 130, 134, 137, 138 | General layout, keybindings, viewport, tabs, shortcuts header, format descriptions, shortcuts obviousness |
| [`tui-theme.md`](tui-theme.md) | 102, 105, 115, 117, 118, 119, 127, 129 | Colors, lipgloss background, `theme.*` helpers, language |
| [`tui-forms.md`](tui-forms.md) | 103, 104, 113, 114, 120, 121, 131, 132, 133, 135, 140 | Forms, modals, focus, status icons, value cycling, WrappedInput, key assignment, invalid field |
| [`tui-tables.md`](tui-tables.md) | 106, 116, 122, 125, 136, 139 | Tables, column widths, plain-text cells + color via `Style`, filter bar, body never replaced (loading or message) |
| [`tui-behavior.md`](tui-behavior.md) | 109, 110, 126, 128 | Bubble Tea (Cmd/Update), scan cache, footer messages (three levels, one component) |

## Critical rules (summary)

**Rule 110** — NEVER modify the model inside a `Cmd` → race condition. Only `Update()` modifies the model.

**Rule 122** — `Cell` returns plain text (it gets measured), color goes through `Style`. A `style.Render(...)` inside `Cell` gets truncated in the middle of its escape sequence and bleeds onto every following row.

**Rule 128** — A footer message goes through `components.FooterMessage`: three levels (neutral info, orange warning, red error), always centered, a single implementation. A table's loading state is shown in the footer, never in the body: with the shared activity dot (`Status.Activity`, `●`/`○`, `SetBlinkPhase`), for a view's own load as well as for work the router tracks. The braille spinner API is removed (DEVDESK-377): nothing under `internal/` imports `bubbles/v2/spinner` or names `Status.Spinner`, `SetSpinnerFrame`, `theme.SpinnerMessage` or `theme.SpinnerStyle` (`TestNoViewImportsTheBubblesSpinner`, `TestRemovedSpinnerSymbolsStayGone`), with no exception. A new `Activity` value not driven by the jobs registry must implement `WantsBlink()`, or the dot stays fixed.

**Rule 139** — A `datatable`'s body is always `m.table.View()`, never a loading screen or a message: an empty table (loading, nothing to list, a filter with no results) stays a table — a header, no rows. The count goes in `GetHeaderInfo`, the status in the footer.

**Rule 129** — All UI text and all logs in **English US**.

**Rule 140** — An invalid form field is underlined through `theme.StyleInvalidField` (the only entry point to the underline API), and the error is also in the footer at level Error, derived on every render. The underline is never the only carrier.

**Rule 133** — `bubbles/textarea` is forbidden. Use `components.WrappedInput` for any multi-line text field.

The per-topic TUI rule files above load when a matching file is read or edited; when reviewing a diff without opening files, read them explicitly.

# Planning Rules

## Implementation Plans

- **Location**: Always write implementation plans to `.claude/plans/` in the current project directory.
- **Format**: Use Markdown format for plans.
- **Naming**: Use descriptive names like `feature-name-plan.md` or `YYYY-MM-DD-feature-name.md`.

## Antigravity IDE Integration

When using the Antigravity IDE extension:
- Save all implementation plans to `.claude/plans/` relative to the project root.
- Create the directory if it doesn't exist before saving plans.
- Plans should be accessible from both Claude Code CLI and Antigravity IDE.

content.content:
1	# Brief — vue graphe git (`git-graph`)
2	
3	Version de découverte, 2026-11-26. Elle consigne ce que l'utilisateur a dit dans la session de découverte, plus des faits lus dans le code. Ni recherche (`researcher`), ni critique (`critic`), ni faisabilité (`architect`) n'ont encore eu lieu : tout ce qui n'est pas marqué « Utilisateur » ou « Code » est une `Hypothèse:`.
4	
5	Convention de lecture : **Utilisateur** = dit ou décidé par l'utilisateur ; **Code** = constaté dans le dépôt ; **Hypothèse:** = proposition du pm, à valider.
6	
7	## Vision (une phrase)
8	
9	Un développeur qui consulte un dépôt git depuis `ws` voit son graphe (commits, branches, tags) dans DevDesk et y fait les opérations git courantes, sans ouvrir un IDE, sans perdre de travail par accident.
10	
11	## Idée brute (Utilisateur)
12	
13	« git-visualiser qui permet d'afficher graphiquement la vue des commit, tags, branches git. Possibilité de faire certaines actions courantes, changer de branche, pull, fetch, etc. À analyser. Cette vue est possible à partir de ws sur un repo git. »
14	
15	Slug validé : `git-graph`.
16	
17	## Problème (Utilisateur)
18	
19	« Ce qui me gêne, c'est de devoir ouvrir l'IDE pour faire de simples opérations git. » L'utilisateur veut **voir** (l'historique, où sont les branches et les tags) **et agir** (les opérations courantes) dans le même écran.
20	
21	Pas de mesure de fréquence ni de preuve extérieure à ce stade. Le seul juge est l'utilisateur (Hypothèse: comme pour `safe-process-stop`, aucune télémétrie connue).
22	
23	## Personas
24	
25	- **Utilisateur (principal)** : développeur DevSecOps qui gère ses dépôts depuis `ws` et ne veut pas basculer vers un IDE pour un checkout, un fetch ou un commit simple.
26	- **Autres utilisateurs du dépôt public** (Utilisateur : « pour lui principalement, mais le dépôt est public ») : le produit sert d'abord l'utilisateur, mais il doit être sûr pour quelqu'un qui ne connaît pas ses habitudes ; d'où l'attention aux garde-fous.
27	
28	## Solutions existantes
29	
30	- **lazygit** (Utilisateur : connu). Hors de son flux : il veut la vue **dans DevDesk**, avec le contexte de `ws`. Le choix de ne pas simplement lancer lazygit depuis DevDesk est donc une décision de l'utilisateur ; les arguments restent à documenter par la recherche.
31	- IDE (VS Code, GoLand...) : la gêne exprimée.
32	- `git log --graph`, `tig`, `gitk`, etc. : non étudiés. À couvrir par `researcher`.
33	- Dans DevDesk (Code) : la vue `ws` affiche déjà une colonne Git Status (`main !3 ?2 ⇡1`) et une colonne Last Tag ; l'action `F` fait un fetch puis un fast-forward avec garde-fous (refus si dépôt sale ou divergé). Le code git passe par la CLI `git` (`internal/git/ops.go`, `internal/git/sync.go`) ; `go.mod` ne contient aucune bibliothèque git en Go.
34	
35	## Périmètre MVP
36	
37	**Variante retenue par l'utilisateur : B (voir + naviguer + travail en cours).** La variante C (historique avancé) est exclue.
38	
39	Point d'entrée (Utilisateur) : la vue s'ouvre depuis `ws`, sur un dépôt git.
40	
41	Dans le périmètre (Utilisateur), par groupe :
42	
43	1. **Voir** : graphe des commits avec branches et tags.
44	2. **Branches et checkout** : changer de branche, créer une branche, supprimer une branche, voir les branches distantes.
45	3. **Synchroniser** : fetch, pull, push.
46	4. **Travail en cours** : diff, stage/unstage, commit, stash.
47	
48	Garde-fous (Utilisateur, exigence forte) : ne pas perdre de travail. Cas cités : checkout avec modifications locales, pull sur dépôt sale ou divergé, push, suppression de branche, stash, commit. Confirmations quand l'action est destructive ou irréversible ; refus avec la raison dans le pied de page (même mécanique que `F` aujourd'hui).
49	
50	Hypothèse: les garde-fous réutilisent et étendent ceux de `internal/git/sync.go` plutôt que d'en créer d'autres, et le détail de chaque règle est fixé dans les stories (une règle testable par opération).
51	
52	## Non-objectifs
53	
54	Écartés par l'utilisateur « pour l'instant » :
55	
56	- merge, rebase, cherry-pick, reset ;
57	- résolution de conflits ;
58	- historique avancé (variante C).
59	
60	Hypothèse: aussi hors périmètre tant que l'utilisateur ne dit pas le contraire : reflog, blame, recherche dans l'historique, gestion des remotes (ajout, suppression), des sous-modules, réécriture d'historique (amend, force-push), interface de gestion des tags (création, suppression ; les tags sont affichés, pas édités). À confirmer.
61	
62	## Hypothèses à valider
63	
64	| # | Hypothèse | Comment la valider |
65	|---|---|---|
66	| H1 | Le besoin est réel et fréquent au point de justifier une vue dédiée plutôt qu'un lancement de lazygit depuis DevDesk | Utilisateur : la gêne est exprimée, la fréquence n'est pas mesurée ; l'utilisateur est le seul juge. La recherche (`researcher`) documente les alternatives |
67	| H2 | Le graphe reste lisible et rapide sur les dépôts réels de l'utilisateur (nombre de commits, branches, tags) | Mesurer sur quelques dépôts ; charger par pages (Hypothèse:) plutôt que tout l'historique. Spike de l'architect |
68	| H3 | La CLI `git` suffit (sortie `--format` stable, pas de bibliothèque Go) | Cohérent avec `internal/git/ops.go` (Code). Faisabilité de l'architect : coût de l'analyse d'un graphe via `git log --graph` ou via `git log --format` plus calcul de la mise en page |
69	| H4 | Les garde-fous de `F` se généralisent à checkout, pull, push, suppression, stash et commit | Analyse de `internal/git/sync.go` par l'architect ; une règle par opération dans les stories |
70	| H5 | La vue peut s'ouvrir sur Linux, Windows natif, macOS et WSL sans comportement divergent | Faisabilité ; mesurer sous Windows natif (chemins, fins de ligne, coût du lancement de `git`) |
71	| H6 | Le succès se juge sur l'usage de l'utilisateur, pas sur une mesure | Hypothèse: à confirmer (voir Métriques) |
72	
73	## Métriques de succès
74	
75	Hypothèse: aucune télémétrie dans DevDesk (à confirmer), donc des garanties testables plus un jugement.
76	
77	1. **Zéro perte de travail** : aucune opération du périmètre n'écrase ni ne supprime de modifications non sauvegardées, de commit non poussé ou de branche non fusionnée sans une confirmation explicite qui le dit. Vérifiable par des tests sur dépôts temporaires, un cas par garde-fou.
78	2. **Refus lisible** : tout refus affiche sa raison dans le pied de page (`components.FooterMessage`), aucun échec silencieux.
79	3. **Jugement de l'utilisateur** : il n'ouvre plus l'IDE pour les opérations du périmètre (son propre constat à l'usage, un mois après livraison). Hypothèse: seule mesure de succès.
80	
81	## Risques
82	
83	| Risque | Gravité | Mitigation |
84	|---|---|---|
85	| Perte de travail par une action mal gardée (checkout avec modifications, suppression de branche non fusionnée, stash, commit au mauvais endroit) | Élevée : c'est la peur déclarée de l'utilisateur | Garde-fous par opération, confirmations, refus avec raison, tests sur dépôts réels temporaires |
86	| Dérive vers un client git complet (merge, rebase, conflits...) | Élevée | Non-objectifs explicites ; variante B figée ; tout ajout passe par l'utilisateur |
87	| Performance du graphe sur un gros dépôt | Moyenne | Chargement paginé, spike de mesure (H2) |
88	| Opérations réseau (fetch, pull, push) : authentification, hors ligne, délais | Moyenne | Voir questions ouvertes ; opérations sans bloquer l'interface (Rule 110, jobs registry) |
89	| Dérive de coût d'entretien : une surface git de plus à maintenir en parallèle de `F` | Moyenne | Réutiliser `internal/git` ; une seule implémentation par opération |
90	| Comportement divergent selon la plateforme | Moyenne | H5, tests sur chaque OS de la CI |
91	| Concurrence avec un IDE ou un autre processus qui modifie le dépôt en même temps (`index.lock`, état changé entre l'affichage et l'action) | Moyenne | Hypothèse: revérifier l'état juste avant chaque action ; message clair si `index.lock` |
92	
93	## Questions ouvertes et hypothèses à valider
94	
95	Ce que seul l'utilisateur peut trancher, ou ce que la faisabilité doit éclairer. Rien n'est décidé ici : chaque réponse proposée est une `Hypothèse:`.
96	
97	1. **Touche d'entrée depuis `ws`.** Quelle touche ouvre la vue sur la ligne d'un dépôt ? Hypothèse: à choisir parmi les touches libres de `ws` (Rule 135, tableau des touches dans `internal/ui/keymap`), à vérifier par l'architect. Que faire sur un dossier qui n'est pas un dépôt git (grisé avec la raison, Rule 130) ?
98	2. **Plateformes.** Linux, macOS, Windows natif, WSL : toutes dans le MVP, ou Linux et macOS d'abord ? Hypothèse: toutes, avec `git` en CLI, à valider par la mesure sous Windows (H5).
99	3. **Taille de dépôt et performance du graphe.** Jusqu'à quelle taille la vue doit-elle rester fluide ? Hypothèse: chargement paginé (par exemple les N derniers commits, plus à la demande) ; le seuil est à fixer par mesure.
100	4. **CLI `git` ou bibliothèque Go.** Hypothèse: CLI, comme le reste de `internal/git` (aucune bibliothèque dans `go.mod` ; ajouter `go-git` serait une dépendance de plus et une seconde implémentation à côté de la CLI). Le comportement de la CLI dépend de la version de `git` installée : version minimale à fixer.
101	5. **Hors ligne.** Que fait la vue sans réseau ? Hypothèse: le graphe local reste utilisable, fetch, pull et push échouent avec la raison dans le pied de page.
102	6. **Authentification pour pull, fetch, push.** DevDesk a son propre stockage de secrets (`internal/credentials`, forge). Hypothèse: la vue ne gère aucune authentification, elle s'appuie sur la configuration git de la machine (assistant d'identifiants, clés SSH) comme `F`. Cas à trancher : un git qui demande un mot de passe sur le terminal pendant que le TUI tient l'écran.
103	7. **Dépôts avec sous-modules ou worktrees.** Hypothèse: un worktree est un dépôt comme un autre ; les sous-modules sont affichés comme un changement de pointeur mais non gérés. À confirmer. Le dépôt de DevDesk lui-même utilise des worktrees sous `.worktrees/` : comportement attendu quand `ws` les liste ?
104	8. **Signature de commits (GPG, SSH).** Hypothèse: la configuration git de la machine s'applique ; si la signature exige une interaction (phrase de passe), l'opération est refusée ou déléguée, à trancher.
105	9. **Hooks git** (pre-commit, pre-push). Hypothèse: ils s'exécutent normalement ; leur sortie et leur échec sont montrés ; l'option `--no-verify` n'est pas proposée. À valider, notamment pour un hook interactif ou long.

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

## Reference

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in
    change  ->  entire graph diff --base A --head B --json
    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **AI Collaboration Rule**:
> - **Planning**, **Brainstorming**, **Implementation** and **Bug fixes** are all
>   in scope. Planning is no longer delegated to Gemini (Antigravity).
> - Implementation plans go in `.claude/plans/` (see
>   [rules/planning.md](rules/planning.md)); design decisions that outlive a plan
>   are recorded in `docs/backlog.md`. Open work (stories, tasks, bugs) is tracked
>   in Plane, see the `## Plane` section of the root `CLAUDE.md`.
> - Always refer to [project-context.md](../project-context.md) for global project rules.
>   It sits in this repository, at the root. The absolute path this line used to
>   carry named a GitLab checkout that is no longer where DevDesk lives.

## Project Overview

DevDesk is a terminal-based TUI (Text User Interface) application built with Go and Bubble Tea framework. It provides DevSecOps functionality including:
- System status monitoring (HTTP/HTTPS, ICMP, DNS, SSL checks)
- GitLab integration (authentication, project explorer, multi-select clone)
- Security scanning (Trivy CVE/secret/license/misconfig + Gitleaks secrets)
- Container management with real-time metrics, on Docker or Podman (`app.container_engine`)
- OCI resource management (image scanning, container launching, network inspection)
- Network diagnostics (DNS, route, ICMP, TCP, TLS, HTTP; a Proxy row says whether a proxy variable applies, the checks themselves stay direct, DEVDESK-582) + real-time port monitoring (`K` stops a process: SIGTERM, up to 5 s, then a confirmed SIGKILL on Linux and macOS, at once on Windows; DevDesk itself, its direct parent, PID 1 and Windows PIDs 0 and 4 are refused; the identity is checked at each signal, DEVDESK-711) + this machine's interfaces + local port forwarding (unprivileged, loopback only) + a path trace under Diagnostics (Trace Path button, or `H` on the route row; no separate tab since DEVDESK-471) (native path trace, on native Linux, native Windows (IPv4 only, ICMP echoes through `iphlpapi`, DEVDESK-486) and WSL2: on macOS and WSL1 the button, `H`, `enter` and `ctrl+o` are greyed and the footer says why, DEVDESK-334; the column starts with this machine, its interface and its gateway; `ctrl+o` can start it from a running Docker Engine container instead (container and network rows, hops still traced from this machine); `H` on the Diagnostics route row opens the trace level on that host without starting it (greyed with the reason on an unsupported platform or a target the trace refuses; its interface and gateway rows reuse the Local route check's reading of the same address, read once, DEVDESK-473), and in the trace level `enter` starts or restarts it, `ctrl+o` picks the source, `esc` cancels then goes back where it came from; under WSL2 the source row says `WSL2 (VM), not the Windows host` with the networking mode, and in NAT mode the gateway and TTL 1 hop are tagged `Windows host (virtual switch)` only when proven, DEVDESK-333; the interface row says `no route` when the kernel proves there is none and `undetermined` when the routing table could not be read, a no-route error keeps the local rows, a trace that ends on the hop limit or the deadline folds its silent tail into one `silent` row and marks the `last to answer` hop, and the target refuses a `:port`, DEVDESK-335)
- Multi-context configuration management via YAML
- Local workspaces management with git metadata
- Claude Code session list (`:agent-usage` / `:au`): sessions found on this machine, by project and date, and per session the agent tree (orchestrator and sub-agents: types, models, tokens, share of the total; sortable by Total; also per agent a state (running / idle / done / unknown, idle after 5 min without a transcript line) shown as a status dot in the first column (the `running` dot blinks, DEVDESK-151) and as text, tool calls and duration; and an indicative cost per agent, `Est. cost` (orange from 75 % and red from 90 % of the session's estimated cost, when at least two agents are priced), from prices you write in the context YAML (`agent_usage.prices`, none shipped), with the session's `Billed` cost and `Unattributed` in the header, DEVDESK-47; a `Breakdown` colour bar per agent and, with `tab` inside a session, a Breakdown tab splitting the whole session's tokens by category, model and agent, as a percentage of tokens, DEVDESK-98). An open session updates live: read again every 2 s while active, only what was appended; paused after 5 min with no write and no unfinished sub-agent, when its transcript is gone, or while the terminal is not focused (header `Updates › paused`, then `paused (terminal not focused)`; `app.when_unfocused: run` keeps it live); `ctrl+r` reads it again in full. The sessions list itself is not live.

## Build and Development Commands

Tasks live in `mise.toml` — there is no Makefile. `mise tasks` lists them all.

```bash
# Development (fastest)
mise run dev          # Run directly with go run
go run .

# Build
mise run build        # Build binary to bin/dk
mise run run          # Build and run

# Testing
mise run test         # Run all tests
mise run cover        # Coverage per package
go test -v ./...      # Run all tests with verbose output
go test ./internal/command  # Run tests for specific package
mise run test-race    # Detect race conditions (critical for Bubble Tea Cmds)

# Code Quality
mise run fmt          # Format code
mise run vet          # Run go vet
mise run lint         # MANDATORY before commits - golangci-lint
mise run tidy         # Tidy dependencies
mise run check        # fmt + vet + lint + test in one go
mise run ci           # the five checks in order (fmt-check, vet, lint, build, test-race), stops at the first failure; unlike check it rewrites no file and also runs build and test-race. `test-race` is the only test run (`-race` covers `go test`); `mise run test` stays available alone for the fast local loop. CI runs fmt-check, vet, lint and build in the `Lint and build` job and `test-race` in the `Test` job, on every pull request, docs-only ones included (the docs-only shortcut applies to `Lint and build` only); the whole CI targets under 10 minutes, so run this locally before a PR to catch a red check early

# Installation
mise run install      # Install to $GOPATH/bin
```

`test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler (`gcc`/`clang`) on `PATH`.

## Git, worktrees, pull requests — absolute rules

- Work happens in a worktree under `.worktrees/<branch>`, created from `origin/main`; the main checkout stays clean, on `main`.
- Never push directly to `main`: the Entire mirror rejects it, and so does the `main-protection` ruleset. Everything goes through a PR, merged once `Lint and build` and `Test` are green.
- Always use `gh -R anthnel/devdesk` (`origin` is `entire://`). There is one remote, `origin`; do not add a second one pointing at GitHub.
- A red `Entire Gates` check caused by Approvals alone does not block a merge (Findings, Checks, Up to date must stay green).
- In a sandbox, only commit; the host pushes, opens the PR and merges. Whoever creates a worktree removes it (never `git worktree prune` from the other side). The sandbox creates its own worktree; the host never creates one for it.
- Before creating a worktree or branch, pushing, opening/merging a PR or removing a worktree, load the `git-worktree-pr` skill.

## Releases

Only merging the release-please PR publishes a release; never merge it without the user's explicit agreement. After every merge on main, the orchestrating session loads the `release-flow` skill and checks the triggers.

## Architecture

The deep notes live in `docs/architecture/`, one file per area, and they are
**not** `@`-imported: an `@` would inline all of it into every session, which is
the thing this split exists to avoid. Read the file that covers what you are

### Status Monitoring System

**Factory Pattern for Checkers:**
- `internal/status/checker.go` - Main orchestrator
- `internal/status/http_checker.go` - HTTP/HTTPS checks
- `internal/status/icmp_checker.go` - ICMP ping checks
- `internal/status/dns_checker.go` - DNS resolution checks

Each checker implements `CheckerInterface`. The main `Checker.CheckOne()` uses a factory pattern to instantiate the right checker based on `component.Type`.

**Parallel Execution:**
- `CheckAll()` runs all component checks concurrently using goroutines and sync.WaitGroup
- Results are collected and returned as `[]ComponentStatus`

### Component CRUD Operations

Status view supports adding/editing/deleting monitors:
- `internal/ui/status/components/component_form.go` - Form component
- `internal/ui/status/components/confirm_modal.go` - Confirmation dialog
- Changes persist to `~/.devdesk/config.yaml` via `config.Save()`

State flags in Model: `creating`, `editing`, `confirming`, `selectedIdx`

### Credentials Management

No secret DevDesk holds is written to a file DevDesk owns. `internal/credentials`
implements the `Storage` interface three ways and `Select()` picks exactly one —
writing to several at once is what let the old "secure" option store a token in
the credential manager *and* in plaintext:

| Storage | Backend | Notes |
|---------|---------|-------|
| `KeyringStorage` | Windows Credential Manager / macOS Keychain / Secret Service | via `zalando/go-keyring`, no cgo. The default. |
| `GitCredentialStorage` | git's configured credential helper | Only when no configured helper is `store` (plaintext) or `cache` (memory with a timeout), by name, path or shell command: `approve` reaches every helper. Context-aware. |
| `MemoryStorage` | this process | Last resort, and deliberately worse: the auth view says nothing was saved. |

`Select(context, preference)` returns a `Selection{Storage, Backend, Detail}`.
The order is keyring → git credential → memory; `app.secret_backend` in the
context config pins the head of it (`auto`, `keyring`, `git-credential`). A
pinned backend that is unreachable falls through to memory rather than silently
to the other one. Every host store operation (the probe, `Save`, `Load`,
`Delete`) is bounded to 3 s: a store that does not answer, such as a locked
Secret Service waiting on an unlock prompt over SSH, is skipped like an absent
one, `Detail` says so, and it is not asked again while that call is stuck
(`internal/credentials/hoststore_bound.go`, DEVDESK-745).

The router resolves one `Selection` per context and keeps it in
`shared.State.Secrets`. It must be reused for the lifetime of the context — a
second `Select()` call yields a fresh `MemoryStorage` that cannot see what the
first one holds.

`MigrateLegacySecrets` runs at startup and on every context switch: a
`gitlab.token` or `registry.password` left in a context file by an older build
is moved into the store and deleted from the YAML, with the result reported in
the auth view. It takes the `Selection` and moves nothing when it does not
persist (memory), and removes a secret from the YAML only once it reads back
from the store; otherwise it stays and the note says so (DEVDESK-745).

## Testing

Test files follow Go conventions (`*_test.go`):
- `internal/command/parser_test.go` - Command parser tests
- `internal/app/app_test.go` - App router tests

Use table-driven tests where appropriate.

**`go test` does not detect races or explore fuzz targets.** `mise run test` runs
only the fuzz seeds, so `internal/agentusage` concurrency tests
(`TestConcurrent*`) need `mise run test-race`. To explore `FuzzIncrementalMatchesFull`
run `go test -fuzz=FuzzIncrementalMatchesFull -fuzztime=60s ./internal/agentusage`.

**HOME is shared across a test process.** `TestMain` in `internal/app` sets
`HOME` once for the whole process, so under `go test -count=N` a test finds
the files its own previous run wrote (context config, forge index cache), and
it fails from `-count=2` while `-count=1` passes (DEVDESK-36). A test that
writes under HOME isolates it with `t.Setenv("HOME", t.TempDir())` and
`USERPROFILE` too; in `internal/app`, call `isolateHome(t)` from
`harness_test.go` (already done by `routerAt`). `internal/ui/setup` is fixed
(DEVDESK-38): its `isolateHome(t)` helper in `model_test.go` is called by the
tests that write under HOME. Other packages whose TestMain does
`os.Setenv("HOME", …)` may have the same default. To find them:
`grep -rn 'os.Setenv("HOME"' --include=*_test.go`, then `go test -count=2` on each package.

**Never get a "free" port by `net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")`, reading the
port, then `Close()`, and letting the code under test bind it later.** Between
the close and the bind, any `bind(0)` can be handed that very port: an
`httptest.NewServer` in the same test, another test, another process on the
runner. The symptom is an intermittent `address already in use`, mostly in CI
(Linux gave the just-closed port back to about 1 `bind(0)` in 7,000; DEVDESK-35,
D85 in `docs/backlog.md`).

- If the code under test takes a port, call `loopback.ReservePort(t)`
  (`internal/testutil/loopback`). On Linux it holds a socket bound with
  `SO_REUSEADDR`, never listening, until `t.Cleanup`: `bind(0)` and `connect()`
  cannot take the port, but `net.Listen` can.
- Otherwise let the server bind `:0` and read the real port, or keep the
  listener open and hand it to the code under test.
- Off Linux, `ReservePort` keeps the old behavior and the window stays open
  (on Windows Go does not set `SO_REUSEADDR`). That is known, not a local bug.
- `internal/testutil/loopback` is imported from `_test.go` files only; nothing
  enforces it yet.

**Nexus tests replay recorded fixtures (DEVDESK-511, DEVDESK-580).** Three campaigns
in `internal/nexusfixture/fixtures/` (`catalog`, `cachedonly`, `access`) replay through
`fakenexus`: `mise run test` needs no bench, cluster or secret. A `record: pending` file is never
versioned (`TestNoPendingFixtureIsVersioned`); `DEVDESK_FIXTURE_RECORDING=1` only in a local recording session.
`nexus-bench record` without `--state` applies no state filter and can overwrite an `upstream-cut` fixture.
Bench writes go only through `nexus-bench:*` tasks and the guarded `DEVDESK_NEXUS_BENCH_SCENARIOS=1` test.
Dated measures live in `docs/measurements/`; a measure contradicting a criterion or the code is frozen and noted, never fixed in the same PR.

**Scanner containers and the proxy (DEVDESK-583, D164).** Every `run --rm` a scanner
issues goes through `containerRun{…}.cmd()` (`internal/scan/container_run.go`): the proxy
variables travel as `-e NAME` with the value in the child environment, never in argv. The
guard `TestContainerGuard*` (`internal/netproxy/container_guard_test.go`) fails on any other
`"run"` literal; only the two permanent exceptions in that file are allowed. The tests of
`internal/scan`, `internal/app` and `internal/ui/security` neutralise the seams
`proxyForward` / `containerForward` in their `TestMain`, so a developer's `HTTPS_PROXY` does not
change an exact argv. The `TestMain` of `internal/app`
also replaces `detectTools` (`internal/app/scan_tools.go`, production value `scan.Detect`) with an
empty report, so `App.Init` never runs the `trivy`, `gitleaks` and `plumber` of the machine
(DEVDESK-645); `TestInitDoesNotRunTheScannersOfTheHost` and `TestDetectToolsIsScanDetectInProduction`
guard it.
The renderers (helm, kustomize) run with the network cut (DEVDESK-767, D180):
`containerRun.Offline` (`--network none`, no proxy) from an image, `offlineEnviron` from a binary,
except kustomize with `scan.tools.kustomize.allow_remote_bases: true`; a refused remote base is the
K8S-RENDER finding `Overlay does not build: remote base blocked` (`remoteBlocked`). A native kustomize is first gated (`internal/scan/kustomize_gate.go`, DEVDESK-771): only local-path references pass, else that finding or `Overlay not built: its references could not be checked`, and kustomize is not started.

**Tests and the host secret store (DEVDESK-610).** By default `credentials.Select` and
`KeyringAvailable` reach the real keyring of the machine (Secret Service over D-Bus on
Linux); a locked keyring blocks the whole suite until the timeout. A test binary that can
reach them isolates the store: `fakekeyring.Install()` in `TestMain`, then
`fakekeyring.Fresh(t)` (or `FreshUnreachable(t, err)` for a locked keyring) per test, from
`internal/testutil/fakekeyring`. `isolateHome(t)` already calls `Fresh` in `internal/app` and
`internal/ui/setup`. Two guards enforce it: at run time, any keyring or `git credential` call
in a test binary without the fake panics with `DEVDESK-610` and the operation; statically,
`TestHostStoreGuard*` (`internal/credentials/hoststore_guard_test.go`) fails on K1 (go-keyring
imported outside `internal/credentials`), K2 (`SwapHostStoreForTest` in non-test code) and K3
(`fakekeyring` imported by non-test code). The seam is `credentials.HostStore` and
`SwapHostStoreForTest`, reserved for tests (it panics outside a test binary). Limits: the
runtime guard only sees the paths a test runs; the static one misses an aliased package
name, a dynamic import and an external binary; `gitHelperUsable` reads the git config
unguarded; `Install` and `Fresh` are global, so no `t.Parallel`. See
`docs/architecture/configuration.md`, "Testing code that reaches the secret store".

**Tests and real signals (DEVDESK-708, DEVDESK-711).** A test must never signal a real process. In
`internal/ports` the only place that does is `realOS.kill(pid, want, sig)` (`internal/ports/procos.go`),
reached through the `procOS` seam, which also holds `identity` and `probe` (`Probe` reads the state, it
sends no signal). `selfPID`, `parentPID`, `goos` and `now` are seams too. A test substitutes them
(`useFakeOS(t, self, parent, goos)` in `seams_test.go`); in `internal/ui/netdiag` it replaces `processOps`
on the model, so `ports.Kill`, `ports.Terminate` and `ports.Probe` are never reached.
`IdentityForTest` and `DeferredIdentityForTest` panic outside a test binary.
Two guards enforce it: at run time, a real signal in a test binary panics with `DEVDESK-708`
unless the test called `allowRealSignals(t)`, which only a test that kills a child it
started itself may do (`TestKillEndsARealChildProcess`, `TestTerminateEndsARealChildProcess` in
`stop_real_test.go`); statically, `TestOnlyRealOSSendsASignal`
fails on a signalling call (`os.FindProcess`, `syscall.Kill`, `unix.Kill`,
`windows.TerminateProcess`, `.Kill(` or `.Signal(`) outside `(realOS) kill`. Limits: the static
guard misses an aliased import, another package and an external binary; the seams are global, so
no `t.Parallel`. See `docs/architecture/network.md`, "Seams and the signal guard".

**Test input and colour (DEVDESK-199).** Build keys only through
`internal/ui/testutil` (`Key`, `Keys`, `Type`, `Paste`, `Text`, `IsText`), never a
literal `tea.KeyPressMsg` or `tea.Key*`. `Key` returns a
`tea.KeyPressMsg` (`Keys` and `Type` return a message list), `Paste` a `tea.PasteMsg`; `Key` is strict: an unknown name
panics. The space key is built as a key (`Key("space")`), never matched through
`String()` (v1 `" "`, v2 `"space"`). Lip Gloss v2 has no global colour profile (`Style.Render` always emits full
colour), so a test needs no setup to check styling; it reads the SGR or strips it
with `ansi.Strip`. `internal/ui/testutil/source_guard_test.go` fails the suite on a
hand-built key, a `colorprofile` import outside `internal/app/profile_test.go` and
`internal/app/redraw_measure_test.go` or `SetColorProfile` in any `_test.go`. Paste tests
(`internal/app/paste_test.go`, `wrapped_input_test.go`, `component_form_test.go`):
a paste reaches the focused field, newlines become spaces in single-line fields,
and no key action fires (Rule 111).

**Space and key API (DEVDESK-200).** Production code matches the space key as
`keymap.Space`, never `" "`/`"space"`, and reads keys through `String()` only
(no `.Runes`, `.Alt`, `.Paste`, `tea.KeyType` or `tea.Key<Name>`). Update
handlers switch on `tea.KeyPressMsg`, never the `tea.KeyMsg` interface (it also
matches releases). A paste is a `tea.PasteMsg`, not a key (Rule 111). Guards in
`internal/ui/keymap` (`space_scan_test.go`, `legacy_key_scan_test.go`,
`viewport_keymap_scan_test.go`) fail the suite otherwise; limits are listed in
`docs/architecture/app-shell.md`.

## Dependencies

Go 1.27 (`go 1.27.3` in `go.mod`). Key libraries (versions as in `go.mod`):
- `charm.land/bubbletea/v2` (v2.1.1) - TUI framework (v2: `tea.KeyPressMsg`, `tea.PasteMsg`, `View() tea.View`)
- `charm.land/bubbles/v2` (v2.2.2) - Pre-built TUI components (table, textinput, viewport)
- `charm.land/lipgloss/v2` (v2.0.6) - Styling (no global colour profile; colours are `image/color.Color`)
- `github.com/charmbracelet/colorprofile` (v0.4.3) - colour profile `main.go` forces under Windows Terminal (replaces `termenv`)
- `github.com/NimbleMarkets/ntcharts/v2` (v2.9.0) - dashboard sparkline
- `github.com/charmbracelet/x/ansi` - ANSI-safe width, strip and cut
- `gitlab.com/gitlab-org/api/client-go` - GitLab API client
- `github.com/prometheus-community/pro-bing` - ICMP ping functionality (maintained fork of go-ping/ping)
- `github.com/google/go-github/v68` - GitHub API client (§3.6)
- `github.com/libp2p/go-netroute` - which interface a destination leaves by, on all three platforms (§3.44)
- `golang.org/x/sys` - direct (Rule 303): the socket calls of `internal/nettrace` (`IP_TTL`, `IP_RECVERR`, `recvmsg` on the error queue); `x/sys/windows` serves `iphlpapi` (the Windows path trace, `IcmpSendEcho2`)
- `github.com/zalando/go-keyring` - host secret manager (wincred / Keychain / Secret Service), no cgo
- `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` - YAML configuration

## Code Conventions

- Comments: **English only** (Rule 307) — existing French comments are not rewritten wholesale, but any new or edited comment is in English
- Commit messages: **English only** (Rule 307)
- UI text and logs: **English US only** (Rule 129)
- Bubbletea models define their own message types
- Use `theme` package for consistent styling (`internal/ui/theme/`)
- Config changes must call `config.Save()` to persist
- All colors defined in `theme/colors.go`, all styles in `theme/styles.go`
- Message naming: `[ComponentName][Action]Msg` (e.g., `ComponentFormSubmitMsg`)
- Context names: the rule exists twice (`config.ValidateContextName`, `contextcmd.ValidName`); change both or neither (`TestContextNameRulesAgree`). Creation refuses `-`, `new`, `list` (`config.ValidateNewContextName`); loading does not (D91)
- Finding text: any new `Resolution`, `Steps` or `Repro` of a scan finding follows the convention in `docs/architecture/scanning.md` ("Writing a Resolution, Steps and Repro for a new finding"); `Repro` only through `localRepro`, `Steps` only from a `*Steps` function (guards in `internal/scan`)

## Critical Bubble Tea Rules

**NEVER modify model state inside a Cmd** (Rule 110) - Race condition:
- `Update()` is the ONLY place to modify model state
- `View()` is read-only
- `Cmd` functions do I/O and return messages

**NEVER use `style.Render()` inside `table.Row{}`** (Rule 122) - ANSI sequences corrupt all subsequent rows:
- Use plain text: `theme.IconError + " error"` not `theme.StatusErrorStyle.Render(...)`
- Apply row styling via `table.SetStyles(theme.TableStylesForState("error"))`

**Views render through `Render()`** (Bubble Tea v2): a top-level view implements
`Render() string` and `View() tea.View { return tea.NewView(m.Render()) }`; only the
router (`App.View()`) sets terminal state such as `AltScreen` and `BackgroundColor`. Components keep
`View() string`. Colours are `color.Color`; hex literals stay in `theme/colors.go`.

**Update() case extraction**: If a case block exceeds 5 lines, extract to `handle[MessageType]()` method returning `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

# TUI — Rule index

TUI rules are split across 5 topic files:

| File | Rules | Content |
|---------|--------|---------|
| [`tui-layout.md`](tui-layout.md) | 101, 107, 108, 111, 112, 123, 124, 130, 134, 137, 138 | General layout, keybindings, viewport, tabs, shortcuts header, format descriptions, shortcuts obviousness |
| [`tui-theme.md`](tui-theme.md) | 102, 105, 115, 117, 118, 119, 127, 129 | Colors, lipgloss background, `theme.*` helpers, language |
| [`tui-forms.md`](tui-forms.md) | 103, 104, 113, 114, 120, 121, 131, 132, 133, 135, 140 | Forms, modals, focus, status icons, value cycling, WrappedInput, key assignment, invalid field |
| [`tui-tables.md`](tui-tables.md) | 106, 116, 122, 125, 136, 139 | Tables, column widths, plain-text cells + color via `Style`, filter bar, body never replaced (loading or message) |
| [`tui-behavior.md`](tui-behavior.md) | 109, 110, 126, 128 | Bubble Tea (Cmd/Update), scan cache, footer messages (three levels, one component) |

## Critical rules (summary)

**Rule 110** — NEVER modify the model inside a `Cmd` → race condition. Only `Update()` modifies the model.

**Rule 122** — `Cell` returns plain text (it gets measured), color goes through `Style`. A `style.Render(...)` inside `Cell` gets truncated in the middle of its escape sequence and bleeds onto every following row.

**Rule 128** — A footer message goes through `components.FooterMessage`: three levels (neutral info, orange warning, red error), always centered, a single implementation. A table's loading state is shown in the footer, never in the body: with the shared activity dot (`Status.Activity`, `●`/`○`, `SetBlinkPhase`), for a view's own load as well as for work the router tracks. The braille spinner API is removed (DEVDESK-377): nothing under `internal/` imports `bubbles/v2/spinner` or names `Status.Spinner`, `SetSpinnerFrame`, `theme.SpinnerMessage` or `theme.SpinnerStyle` (`TestNoViewImportsTheBubblesSpinner`, `TestRemovedSpinnerSymbolsStayGone`), with no exception. A new `Activity` value not driven by the jobs registry must implement `WantsBlink()`, or the dot stays fixed.

**Rule 139** — A `datatable`'s body is always `m.table.View()`, never a loading screen or a message: an empty table (loading, nothing to list, a filter with no results) stays a table — a header, no rows. The count goes in `GetHeaderInfo`, the status in the footer.

**Rule 129** — All UI text and all logs in **English US**.

**Rule 140** — An invalid form field is underlined through `theme.StyleInvalidField` (the only entry point to the underline API), and the error is also in the footer at level Error, derived on every render. The underline is never the only carrier.

**Rule 133** — `bubbles/textarea` is forbidden. Use `components.WrappedInput` for any multi-line text field.

The per-topic TUI rule files above load when a matching file is read or edited; when reviewing a diff without opening files, read them explicitly.

# Planning Rules

## Implementation Plans

- **Location**: Always write implementation plans to `.claude/plans/` in the current project directory.
- **Format**: Use Markdown format for plans.
- **Naming**: Use descriptive names like `feature-name-plan.md` or `YYYY-MM-DD-feature-name.md`.

## Antigravity IDE Integration

When using the Antigravity IDE extension:
- Save all implementation plans to `.claude/plans/` relative to the project root.
- Create the directory if it doesn't exist before saving plans.
- Plans should be accessible from both Claude Code CLI and Antigravity IDE.

1	# Recherche — process-list (2026-11-22)
2	
3	Source : agent `product-team:researcher`, sources consultées le 2026-11-22. Étiquettes : [S] établi par une source, [I] inférence, [ND] aucune donnée trouvée. Condensé par l'orchestrateur ; les URL sont en fin de fichier.
4	
5	## Synthèse
6	
7	1. Les métriques (CPU, mémoire) sont le cœur de « remplacer le gestionnaire de tâches » ; elles sont faisables avec gopsutil, mais le CPU % exige deux échantillons. [I]
8	2. Le marché est saturé en lecture, pas en intégration : tous les outils font tri, recherche et arrêt ; seul bottom couvre Linux, macOS et Windows en TUI avec signaux et arbre. L'apport d'un écran DevDesk serait le contexte (lien avec Ports, ses propres port-forwards et scans, conteneurs), non démontré par une source. [I]
9	3. L'arrêt « propre » n'est pas symétrique : SIGTERM sous Unix ; sous Windows, gopsutil ne fait que `TerminateProcess`. [S]
10	4. gopsutil ne vérifie pas l'identité du processus avant de signaler : risque de PID réutilisé réel. [S]
11	
12	## Alternatives
13	
14	| Outil | Plateformes | Établi | Limites |
15	|---|---|---|---|
16	| htop | Linux, BSD, macOS, Solaris ; pas Windows [S] | visionneuse interactive | kill, arbre, recherche non confirmés par la page lue |
17	| btop | Linux, macOS, BSD ; pas de Windows natif [S] | signal au choix, arbre, filtre | macOS : suid root recommandé pour les processus des autres |
18	| bottom | Linux, macOS, Windows [S] | tri, recherche, signaux, arbre | Windows : `TerminateProcess(handle, 1)`, pas d'arrêt propre [S] |
19	| procs | Linux, Windows ; macOS « experimental » [S] | recherche multi-colonnes, ports, conteneur Docker, arbre, `watch` | kill non mentionné ; macOS : rien sur les processus des autres sans sudo |
20	| glances | Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, Windows [S] | liste filtrable, conteneurs, API REST, serveur MCP | kill non confirmé |
21	| gotop | Linux, FreeBSD, macOS ; Windows « limited testing » [S] | liste de processus | kill et tri non confirmés |
22	| Process Explorer | Windows [S] | handles, DLL, comptes | GUI Windows seule |
23	| Gestionnaire des tâches Windows | Windows | [ND] page non consultée | |
24	| Activity Monitor | macOS [S] | « Quit » (peut être refusé) / « Force Quit » | un processus d'autrui peut demander une authentification admin |
25	| taskkill | Windows [S] | `/f` force, `/t` arbre | sans `/f`, `WM_CLOSE` aux fenêtres du PID (winquit) |
26	| ntop, « k9s-like » pour processus | [ND] | | non identifiés |
27	
28	## Preuves du problème
29	
30	- Pour : serveurs de dev orphelins (`EADDRINUSE`, geste standard `lsof -i :PORT` puis `kill`, SIGTERM avant `kill -9`) ; `kubectl port-forward` oubliés (`pkill -f`, issue « Orphaned kubectl.exe processes on Windows »). [S, articles communautaires] L'onglet Ports de DevDesk les couvre déjà quand le processus tient un socket (`internal/ports/ports.go`). [S]
31	- Contre ou non démontré : aucune donnée sur la fréquence du besoin ni sur les utilisateurs de DevDesk qui quittent le TUI pour un gestionnaire de tâches ; aucune preuve que les processus sans socket qui consomment soient un problème fréquent. [ND]
32	
33	## Faits techniques (gopsutil v4.26.7, version de `go.mod`)
34	
35	- Linux : PID via `/proc`, ligne de commande `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, mémoire `statm`, CPU `stat`, UID `status` ; `Processes()` saute les processus qui échouent. [S]
36	- macOS : `sysctl kern.proc.all`, `kern.procargs2`, `proc_pidinfo` (échecs ignorés pour mémoire et CPU) ; `Cwd` renvoie `ErrorNotPermitted` pour les processus inaccessibles ; sans sudo, procs ne donne rien sur les processus des autres. [S]
37	- Windows : PID via `EnumProcesses` ; CPU, mémoire, utilisateur via `OpenProcess` (`PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION`) ; ligne de commande via le PEB, chaîne vide sans erreur si accès refusé ; `SendSignal` renvoie `ErrNotImplementedError`, `Terminate`/`Kill` = `TerminateProcess`, aucun arrêt propre. [S]
38	- Dépôt : 294 processus nommés en 11 ms sous Windows par snapshot Toolhelp32 (commentaire de `ports.go`) ; la lecture par PID donne « Access denied » pour 98 sockets sur 189 sans élévation. [S, dépôt]
39	- CPU % : `Percent(0)` renvoie 0 au premier appel, puis le delta CPU / temps écoulé × 100 (pas ramené à 100 %) ; `CPUPercent()` est la moyenne sur la vie du processus. Il faut garder les objets `Process` entre deux rafraîchissements. [S, I]
40	- Coût d'une énumération complète avec métriques : aucun benchmark trouvé ; linéaire en nombre de processus. [ND, I]
41	- Arrêt propre sous Windows : `os.Process.Signal(Interrupt)` non implémenté en Go ; `CTRL_C_EVENT` ne vise pas un groupe précis ; `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` ne marche que pour un groupe créé par `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` partageant la console ; `WM_CLOSE` sur les fenêtres (ce que fait taskkill sans `/f`, et winquit) : ignoré par une application console ou bloquée, limité à la session. 4	
5	## Synthèse
6	
7	1. Les métriques (CPU, mémoire) sont le cœur de « remplacer le gestionnaire de tâches » ; elles sont faisables avec gopsutil, mais le CPU % exige deux échantillons. [I]
8	2. Le marché est saturé en lecture, pas en intégration : tous les outils font tri, recherche et arrêt ; seul bottom couvre Linux, macOS et Windows en TUI avec signaux et arbre. L'apport d'un écran DevDesk serait le contexte (lien avec Ports, ses propres port-forwards et scans, conteneurs), non démontré par une source. [I]
9	3. L'arrêt « propre » n'est pas symétrique : SIGTERM sous Unix ; sous Windows, gopsutil ne fait que `TerminateProcess`. [S]
10	4. gopsutil ne vérifie pas l'identité du processus avant de signaler : risque de PID réutilisé réel. [S]
11	
12	## Alternatives
13	
14	| Outil | Plateformes | Établi | Limites |
15	|---|---|---|---|
16	| htop | Linux, BSD, macOS, Solaris ; pas Windows [S] | visionneuse interactive | kill, arbre, recherche non confirmés par la page lue |
17	| btop | Linux, macOS, BSD ; pas de Windows natif [S] | signal au choix, arbre, filtre | macOS : suid root recommandé pour les processus des autres |
18	| bottom | Linux, macOS, Windows [S] | tri, recherche, signaux, arbre | Windows : `TerminateProcess(handle, 1)`, pas d'arrêt propre [S] |
19	| procs | Linux, Windows ; macOS « experimental » [S] | recherche multi-colonnes, ports, conteneur Docker, arbre, `watch` | kill non mentionné ; macOS : rien sur les processus des autres sans sudo |

49	- Processus critiques : PID 1 ne reçoit que les signaux qu'il gère ; certains processus Windows protégés refusent même un administrateur (non vérifié par une source). [S, ND]
50	- Enfants : `Process.Kill` ne tue pas les enfants ; `taskkill /t` tue l'arbre. [S]

content.content:
**What undo can do**
- Undo and redo commit and branch actions: press `z` to undo and `Z` (shift+z) to redo.
- Walk back through the reflog step by step, so you don't need to read it yourself. For example, it reverts checkouts, commits being applied, and interactive rebases.
- Undo actions taken outside lazygit, such as on the command line.
- Remember your place in the undo history after you quit and reopen lazygit.

**What undo cannot do**
- Recover changes to the working tree or the stash, since these aren't recorded in the reflog.
- Reverse permanent actions, such as pushing to a remote.
- Undo branch creation, since it isn't stored in the reflog.
- Work during a rebase. The page recommends aborting the rebase instead, using `m` for the rebase options.

**Warnings about losing work**
- Uncommitted changes and stash entries are outside undo's scope, so mistakes involving them may not be recoverable through this feature.
- Pushed commits stay pushed.
- The feature is new and may have bugs. If something goes wrong, you may need to check the reflog and restore your position manually.

Git is a distributed version control system (VCS) that tracks a project's change history, so earlier versions can be recovered and team members can see who changed what, when, and why. Each developer holds a full copy of the project and its history, so no constant connection to a central server is needed.

- **Repositories** contain a project's files and their revision history. Changes are saved as commits, which can be organized into branches.
- **GitHub** hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration tools such as issues, pull requests, code review, and a marketplace of apps. Its GitHub flow is to create a branch, commit changes, open a pull request for discussion, and merge once the team agrees.
- **Common commands** include `git init` (start tracking a directory), `git clone` (copy a remote project), `git add` (stage changes), `git commit` (save a snapshot), `git branch`, `git merge`, `git pull` (sync from the remote), and `git push` (upload local commits).
- **Collaboration models** are a shared repository, where contributors get explicit read, write, or admin access, and fork and pull, where anyone can copy a project, make changes, and propose them through a pull request for maintainer review.

Search results point to a few known go-git slowdowns on large repositories, mostly in `Status()` and commit iteration:

- **Commit iteration (go-git issue 1294):** One reporter found that iterating commit objects was about 16 times slower than the raw git command. The same report describes a multi-second freeze at a specific commit. The reporter expected some overhead from the custom objects go-git creates, but considered the gap larger than that would explain.
- **Status on large worktrees (go-git issue 993):** A contributor measured Status() taking about 5 seconds in a large repository. Their proposed workaround was to skip the full status check when a specific path is being added.
- **Untracked files (go-git issue 181):** A related issue, cited from another project's tracker, notes that Status() is slow with a large number of untracked files.
- **Maintainer's stated expectations:** An older go-git performance talk says most operations on small and medium sizes spend less than twice the time the git command takes. It also says the team was adding optimizations such as modifying an LRU cache to evict more than one object when space runs short. That talk predates the current code, so treat its numbers as dated.
- **Gitea experience:** A Gitea thread found that a go-git native approach was faster than the git CLI for the root directory, but there was still a slowdown problem in subdirectories. So results vary by operation and path.

Overall, the evidence is mostly issue reports, not current benchmarks. Status and large-history commit walks are the main slow spots. I did not find a current go-git release note confirming these have been fixed, so check the latest go-git issues and run your own timing on your repository before relying on go-git for these operations.

## Overview

The graph is built in two passes. First, `GetPipeSets` computes a list of **pipes** for each commit row. Then `RenderAux` turns each row's pipes into a line of **cells** of text.

## Pipes (the lane model)

A `Pipe` is a line segment between two columns, with `fromPos`/`toPos` as column indexes. Its `kind` is one of:

- **STARTS**: begins at a commit's column and goes to the commit's parent. Merges add extra STARTS pipes, one per additional parent.
- **CONTINUES**: passes through a row, carrying a line toward a commit further down.
- **TERMINATES**: ends at the current commit's column.

Pipes are the only state carried between rows. The first row starts with one pipe from a synthetic `START` hash to the first commit at column 0.

## Processing each commit (`getNextPipes`)

1. **Drop stale pipes.** Pipes that terminated on the previous row are removed, as is the pipe into the empty-tree hash, since nothing follows a root commit.
2. **Choose the commit's column (`pos`).** It defaults to one past the rightmost column in use. If an existing pipe targets this commit, `pos` is that pipe's column, so the commit sits under its first child.
3. **Add the STARTS pipe** from `pos` to the commit's first parent, or to the empty tree for a root commit.
4. **Handle incoming pipes:**
   - Pipes targeting this commit become TERMINATES pipes that run to `pos`.
   - Pipes to the left of `pos` become CONTINUES pipes that may shift left into the lowest free column.
   - Extra merge parents get STARTS pipes in the lowest column that is neither taken nor traversed by a continuing pipe.
   - Pipes to the right of `pos` become CONTINUES pipes that slide left into any blank columns.
5. **Sort** the row's pipes by `toPos`, then `kind`. The code comment admits this is "not efficient but doing it for now."

Two sets track occupancy during this step. `takenSpots` holds columns where a pipe ends. `traversedSpots` holds columns a pipe starts on, ends on, or passes through.

## Rendering (`RenderCommitGraph` → `RenderAux` → `renderPipeSet`)

- **Parallelism:** `RenderAux` splits the rows into `GOMAXPROCS` contiguous chunks, renders them in goroutines, and concatenates the results in order. Rendering a row needs only the row's pipes and the previous commit, so chunks are independent.
- **Cells:** each row gets one cell per column up to the rightmost pipe. A cell records up, down, left, and right connections and a style. Horizontal segments fill the cells between a pipe's endpoints, and vertical segments are set at its ends.
- **Commit position and type:** the commit's column comes from its STARTS pipe, or from a TERMINATES pipe if it has no STARTS. The cell is marked MERGE when there are two or more STARTS pipes, and COMMIT otherwise.
- **Draw order:** non-selected STARTS pipes are drawn first, then other non-selected pipes. Selected-commit pipes are drawn last so they override the others.
- **Selection highlight:** if the previous row was the selected commit and no visible pipe links the selected commit, highlighting is suppressed. This keeps two adjacent commits from both lighting up.
- **Symbol-set differences:**
  - With box-drawing symbols, cells under selected pipes are reset first because those characters can't combine lines. Each cell shows only the highlighted lines.
  - With branch-drawing symbols, a highlighted horizontal line that crosses another commit's vertical line is drawn over it.
- **Root commits:** the line below a root commit is removed.

## Limits

- Column positions are `int16`, which caps the number of lanes.
- Hash equality is by pointer, so it is only correct if every hash comes from a shared pool. The code says so: "all hashes are stored in the pool."
- A commit's position depends on the order of the input commits and on the previous row's pipes, so the layout can't be computed for an arbitrary row in isolation.
- Each row's pipes are rebuilt from the previous row's pipes, so the full pipe list must be computed in order before rendering.

- **Version:** 1.30.0 (taken from the extension's icon URL path)

`gh pr checkout` checks out a pull request in git. You can specify it by PR number, URL, or branch name, and it works for PRs from forks. Options include setting a local branch name, checking out with a detached HEAD, and checking out into a worktree.

The page doesn't say anything about gh's license, so I can't confirm that it's MIT licensed based on this content.

**Checkout branch**
- `<space>` (Local branches): Checkout selected item
- `c` (Local branches): Checkout by name
- `-` (Local branches): Checkout previous branch
- `F` (Local branches): Force checkout, which discards local changes first
- `<space>` (Remote branches): Check out a new local branch from the selected remote branch

**Delete branch**
- `d` (Local branches): View delete options for local or remote branch
- `d` (Remote branches): Delete the remote branch from the remote

**Discard changes**
- `d` (Files): View options for discarding changes to the selected file
- `d` (Main panel, normal): Discard the selected change. Unstaged changes are discarded; staged changes are unstaged.

**Stash**
- `s` (Files): Stash all changes
- `S` (Files): View stash options
- `<space>` (Stash): Apply the stash entry
- `g` (Stash): Pop the stash entry
- `d` (Stash): Drop the stash entry

**Force push**
- No dedicated force push keybinding appears in the content. `P` is the regular Push.

**Reset**
- `g` (Commits, Local branches, Reflog, Remote branches): Reset onto the selected item
- `D` (Files): Reset options for the working tree
- `g` (Files): View upstream reset options

**Nuke working tree**
- `D` (Files): Reset options for the working tree, described as "nuking the working tree"

**Undo**
- `z` (Global): Undo the last git command, based on the reflog
- `Z` (Global): Redo

**License:** The page links to a LICENSE file but doesn't name the license type.

**Features:**
- **Checkout:** Yes. Branches can be checked out, and commits can be checked out from the graph.
- **Delete branch:** Yes. The page lists "Delete" among branch actions.
- **Merge:** Yes. Merge is available for both branches and commits.
- **Stash:** Yes. The page lists "Apply, Create Branch From, Drop & Pop Stashes" and "Clean, Reset & Stash Uncommitted Changes."
- **Force push:** Not mentioned. The page lists "Push" for branches and tags but says nothing about force push.

**Installs:** The extension is "available on the Visual Studio Marketplace for Visual Studio Code," and the page links to its listing. It shows no install count.

**Maintenance status and last release:** The page doesn't give a release date or version. The Releases section is empty in the captured content. It shows 447 commits, 319 open issues, 21 open pull requests, and a 2026 copyright footer. It doesn't say the project is archived or unmaintained.

I ran one search. It turned up only a little lazygit-specific material, and nothing from lazygit's official docs.

- **Lazygit autostash:** A git-how tutorial says lazygit has an autostash feature. When you check out a branch with uncommitted changes, an Autostash message appears, and confirming it stashes the changes, switches branches, and reapplies them. It also says you may need to resolve conflicts if the stashed files overlap with the new branch. Lazygit offers a straightforward way to handle this situation through its autostash feature. In some cases, you might need to resolve merge conflicts if the changes in the stashed files conflict with the new branch. Lazygit will alert you. This is a third-party tutorial, so check lazygit's own docs for the exact prompt wording.
- **The "would be overwritten" error:** This is plain git behavior. A mailing-list post quotes the error: "Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout". Git only blocks a switch when the switch would touch files you have uncommitted changes in. Git only prevents switching branches if the act of switching branches would modify the files you have uncommitted changes to.
- **Native git autostash:** Git's own `checkout` and `switch` did not have autostash for a long time. A recent Git patch adds `--autostash` to both, along with a `checkout.autostash` config option. "git checkout" and "git switch" require users to manually stash and unstash their changes. Until that lands in a release, the `git checkout --autostash` flag may not be available on your version.
- **Workarounds:** Manual stash-then-checkout works in any git version. One source gives the sequence as stashing your changes in the current branch with git stash, then checking out the branch you want to switch to.

content.content:
**`-d` / `--delete`**

> Delete a branch. The branch must be fully merged in its upstream branch, or in `HEAD` if no upstream was set with `--track` or `--set-upstream-to`.

So `-d` refuses to delete a branch unless its commits are already merged into its upstream, or into `HEAD` if it has no upstream.

**`-D`**

> Shortcut for `--delete` `--force`.

**What `--force` changes**

> In combination with `-d` (or `--delete`), allow deleting the branch irrespective of its merged status, or whether it even points to a valid commit.

So `-D` deletes the branch regardless of whether it is merged, and regardless of whether it points to a valid commit. Git's merge check is the only safeguard `-d` provides, and `-D` skips it.

**Example from the manual**

```
$ git branch -d -r origin/todo origin/html origin/man   # delete remote-tracking branches
$ git branch -D test                                    # delete "test" even if it has unmerged commits
```

The manual notes that `-D` deletes "test" even if the currently checked-out branch does not contain all of its commits.

**The `--delete` safety statement**

The manual gives no separate safety statement for `--delete`. Its only safety-related wording is the merged requirement quoted above. The `-r` option is related: `-r` with `-d` deletes remote-tracking branches, and the manual warns that this "only makes sense ... if they no longer exist in the remote repository or if `git fetch` was configured not to fetch them again."

The page loaded. It's the `docs/Config.md` file from the `jesseduffield/lazygit` repository on GitHub's `master` branch. It's the lazygit configuration reference, covering the config file locations, default settings, keybindings, and platform-specific options.

**`--graph`**
- Draws a text graph of the history on the left side of the output. It may insert extra lines between commits so the graph draws correctly.
- It "enables parent rewriting" (see History Simplification).
- "This implies the `--topo-order` option by default, but the `--date-order` option may also be specified."
- It cannot be combined with `--no-walk`.

**Topological order**
- `--topo-order`: "Show no parents before all of its children are shown, and avoid showing commits on multiple lines of history intermixed."
- `--date-order`: no parent before its children, "otherwise show commits in the commit timestamp order."

**Format placeholders**
- `%H`: commit hash
- `%P`: parent hashes
- `%D`: ref names without the " (", ")" wrapping

**`-n` / `--skip`**
- `-<number>`, `-n <number>`, `--max-count=<number>`: "Limit the output to the first <number> commits that would be shown."
- `--skip=<number>`: "Skip <number> commits before starting to show the commit output."

**`--decorate`**
- Values: `short`, `full`, `auto`, `no`.
- `short` omits the `refs/heads/`, `refs/tags/`, and `refs/remotes/` prefixes. `full` prints the full ref name.
- `auto` shows refs as `short` when output goes to a terminal, and none otherwise.
- `--decorate` alone means `--decorate=short`. The default comes from `log.decorate` if set, otherwise `auto`.

**Performance**
- The visible text does not mention `commit-graph`. The content is truncated, so it may appear in the cut-off part.
- The only performance note I can see is for `--simplify-merges`: "requires walking the entire commit history before returning a single result. This can make the option difficult to use for very large repositories."
- The Object Traversal options are described as "mostly targeted for packing of Git repositories."

[WebFetch note: this page's text is 162675 characters long and the answer above covers only characters 0 to 100000; the final 62675 were not read — to read on, call WebFetch again with the same url and offset: 100000.]

**Local modifications**

- **Default:** Switching doesn't require a clean index or working tree, but the operation is aborted if it would lose local changes. The page states: "Switching branches does not require a clean index and working tree (i.e. no differences compared to `HEAD`). The operation is aborted however if the operation leads to loss of local changes, unless told otherwise with `--discard-changes` or `--merge`."

- **`-m` / `--merge`:** Conflicting local changes are stashed before the switch and reapplied afterward. "If the local changes do not overlap with the differences between branches, the switch proceeds without stashing. If reapplying the stash results in conflicts, the entry is saved to the stash list. Resolve the conflicts and run `git stash drop` when done, or clear the working tree (e.g. with `git reset --hard`) before running `git stash pop` later to re-apply your changes."

- **`--conflict=<style>`:** Same as `--merge`, but sets how conflicting hunks are shown. Values are `merge` (default), `diff3`, and `zdiff3`. It overrides `merge.conflictStyle`.

- **`--discard-changes` (alias `-f` / `--force`):** "Proceed even if the index or the working tree differs from `HEAD`. Both the index and working tree are restored to match the switching target." This discards local changes.

- **`-c` / `--create` and `-C` / `--force-create`:** These create the branch before switching. The page doesn't describe any special handling of local changes for these options. The rules above still apply. `-c` is described as transactional: "the branch is not reset/created unless `git switch` is successful." `-C` resets an existing branch to `<start-point>`.

**`--autostash`**

The page does not document an `--autostash` option. The `--merge` example output shows the message `Applied autostash.`, but that is informational output, not a flag you pass.

```
$ git switch -m mytopic
Applied autostash.
Switched to branch 'mytopic'
```

**Version**

The page doesn't state a version for the `--merge` behavior specifically. The version selector shows the page is "last updated in 2.55.0," and the changelog lists "2.55.1 → 2.56.1 no changes," so the content is current as of Git 2.55.x–2.56.x. Run `git --version` to check your installed version.

## Key points from the git-push manual

**`--force-with-lease`**
- Overrides the "must fast-forward" rule only if the remote ref still has the expected value. Otherwise the push fails.
- Forms:
  - `--force-with-lease`: protects all refs being updated. The expected value is the remote-tracking branch.
  - `--force-with-lease=<refname>`: protects one ref, using the remote-tracking value as the expected value.
  - `--force-with-lease=<refname>:<expect>`: protects one ref against an explicit expected value. If `<expect>` is empty, the ref must not already exist.
- Background `git fetch` can silently update remote-tracking refs and defeat the lease. The manual suggests a separate push remote, or an explicit `base` tag:
  ```
  git tag base master
  git rebase -i master
  git push --force-with-lease=master:base master:master
  ```

**`--force-if-includes`**
- Before a forced update, checks that the tip of the remote-tracking ref is reachable from the local branch's reflog, meaning those remote updates were integrated locally.
- Only meaningful with `--force-with-lease` (bare, or `=<refname>`). With `--force-with-lease=<refname>:<expect>` or without `--force-with-lease`, it is a no-op.
- Enable by default with `push.useForceIfIncludes=true`. Override per push with `--no-force-if-includes`.

**`push.default`**
- `nothing`: push nothing unless a refspec is given (error out).
- `current`: push the current branch to a same-named branch on the remote.
- `upstream`: push to the branch that `@{upstream}` points to. Intended for central workflows.
- `tracking`: deprecated synonym for `upstream`.
- `simple`: push the current branch to the same-named remote branch. Requires that an upstream with the same name exists when pushing back to the pulled remote. **Default since Git 2.0.**
- `matching`: push all branches that exist with the same name on both ends. **Was the default before Git 2.0.**

**Behavior when a non-fast-forward push is rejected**
- A push is a fast-forward only if the remote commit A is an ancestor of the new commit B. Otherwise history is lost.
- Git refuses by default. The status line shows `!` with reason `rejected` (client-side) or `remote rejected` (server-side, e.g. `receive.denyNonFastForwards`).
- Fixes, in the manual's order:
  - `git pull` (creates merge commit C), or `git pull --rebase`, then push normally.
  - `git push --force` only if you truly intend to discard history and no one has fetched the old commit.
- `--force` or a leading `+` in the refspec overrides the check. `+` applies to that refspec only. `--force` applies to all refs being pushed.

**`--set-upstream` (`-u`)**
- Adds upstream (tracking) config for every branch that was successfully pushed or was already up to date, so `git pull` and `git status` work without arguments:
  ```
  git push -u origin main
  ```
- `push.autoSetupRemote=true` does this automatically on the first push of a branch when no upstream exists.

Local History automatically records your project's state as you edit, run tests, or deploy, including changes made outside the IDE. It works independently of version control, so it can help even if your project isn't under VCS or you've made changes since your last commit.

You can use it to:
- Restore deleted files.
- Revert a whole file, or a specific code fragment, to an earlier revision.
- Serve as a recovery source if your computer restarts unexpectedly.

By default, it keeps revisions for the last 5 working days, meaning days when the file was modified. You can change this in Advanced Settings (IDE section) or with the `localHistory.daysToKeep` JVM option. Setting it to 0 disables Local History.

The docs also note that Local History is "not a replacement for proper version control." It's cleared when you install a new IDE version, is for personal use only, and isn't guaranteed to keep every revision because of its retention period and size limit.

The page covers the features you asked about, but not the confirmation prompts, settings, or discard recovery.

**Features covered**
- **Source Control Graph:** Inspects commits, branches, and incoming or outgoing work.
- **Branches, stashes, and worktrees:** Branches develop separate lines of work. Stashes set aside uncommitted changes. Worktrees check out another branch in a separate folder.
- **Sync:** Push uploads your commits, pull integrates remote commits, and sync pulls before pushing. The status bar shows the active branch and provides sync actions.

**Not covered**
- **Discard or force-push confirmations:** The page doesn't describe any.
- **`git.confirmForcePush`:** The page doesn't mention this setting.
- **Undoing a discard, including trash or recycle bin recovery:** The page links to "Choose an undo action" under "Undo or recover work," but the linked section isn't included in this content.

The wip modes act as a safety net for **uncommitted** changes, which Git doesn't track. Magit's global `magit-wip-mode` saves "**tracked** files to work-in-progress references after or before certain actions." Untracked files are never saved, and nothing is saved before the first commit exists.

- **Storage:** Snapshots go to two refs per branch: `refs/wip/index/<branchref>` for the staging area and `refs/wip/wtree/<branchref>` for the working tree. With a detached HEAD, `HEAD` replaces `<branchref>`.
- **Recovery:** `magit-wip-log` and `magit-wip-log-current` show a branch's wip history. `X w` (`magit-reset-worktree`) restores the working tree to a chosen commit, and `magit-wip-commit` snapshots all tracked changes on demand.
- **Limits:** It isn't complete protection. Changes made and destroyed outside Emacs may be lost, since Magit never gets a chance to save them.

The page doesn't say whether the mode is enabled by default. It only describes how the mode works when enabled.

- **Mechanism:** tea.ExecProcess(cmd, callback) suspends the TUI, runs the command, then resumes. The docs describe the same sequence: the program releases terminal control, runs the external command, waits for it to finish, restores terminal control, and sends the callback message to Update.
- **Blocking:** ExecProcess blocks the entire Bubble Tea program while the command is running.
- **When to use it:** For non-interactive I/O, a regular tea.Cmd is the better choice. ExecProcess is for interactive programs like lazygit.
- **Suspend alternative:** Bubble Tea's Suspend message exists because raw mode means ctrl+z must be handled per program. This is a different approach from running a child process.
- **Known pitfall:** One issue report describes typing q as the first key sometimes exiting the Go program as soon as vi exits, which suggests leftover keypresses can leak back into the parent TUI.
- **Lazygit itself:** I found no source on how lazygit.nvim launches lazygit or whether it uses a terminal embed or a subprocess. Its own docs describe it as a simple terminal UI for git commands.
